newsitem.title: THAILAND: Battered Thai bourse must find own level - SET head.
newsitem.headline: Battered Thai bourse must find own level - SET head.

text.p: The head of the Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) said the nation's battered share market should be left to find its proper level without interference from the government or support funds.

SET president Singh Tangtatswas told reporters late on Monday that the prolonged bearishness of Thai stocks, now at 51-month-lows, could be attributed to Thailand's weak economic outlook, which might not improve quickly.
"There is a real economic problem. It is going to stay. We should let the market decide where it should be," Singh said.
The composite SET Index closed on Monday at 819.79. By 0450 GMT on Tuesday, the index was up 5.50 points to 825.29.

Singh said Thai brokerage firms and mutual funds had lately shied away from trying to shore up the market partly because of the bourse's 2.52 trillion baht ($100 billion) market capitalisation made it hard for them to intervene.
He said unlike past Thai market crises which were mostly caused by political developments, the SET and brokers believed this decline was influenced mainly by economic factors.
The Thai economy this year is projected to expand 6.7 percent, its slowest pace in a decade.
The Thai current account deficit is expected to widen to a six-year high of 8.2 percent of gross domestic product in 1996 from 8.1 percent in 1995.
Singh said the political uncertainty of the past few months and the time needed for the new coalition of Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh to settle in have also weighed on the market.
"This time it is different. We have to admit that the economy is not doing well and the government has not yet functioned according to its job," he said.

"Although Thai exports and economy may not be much worse than our neighbours, our political stability appears to be in worse shape than others. Even Philippine President Fidel Ramos seems to be in better shape than our government," Singh said.
He said Thai stocks had lost about 34 percent of their market value since he took office last July with the index falling steadily from 1,247 at the end of June this year.

He said the prolonged weakness of Thai stocks had forced retail investors trading on margins to sell an average of 200 million baht a week of their holdings to meet debt obligations since July. ($1 = 25 baht)
